resources.string: Set up phone control

Mika uses apps for you on a separate virtual screen, so you can keep using your phone. For this it borrows Android’s built-in “USB debugging” and “Wireless debugging”: pair once and Mika connects automatically from then on — no computer needed. Web and file tasks work without this. Don’t change any other switch in Developer options unless Mika asks you to: some can erase your phone.
Not now
Phone control
You can skip this for now and just use web, files and chat; Mika will remind you the first time it needs an app.
This environment can’t operate the apps on your phone; chat, web, files and calculations work as usual.
Phone control needs Android’s Developer options and Wireless debugging, and neither is available here.
Turn on Developer options
Open “About phone” in Settings and tap “Build number” 7 times until you see “You are now a developer”. On some phones “Build number” is under “Software information”.
Open About phone
On
Tap “Build number” 7 times in “About phone”
Turn on USB debugging

In “Developer options”, find “USB debugging”, turn it on and tap “OK” when asked. Don’t change the other switches: some can erase your phone. No cable needed: with it on, Mika can keep working even when Wi-Fi is off.
Open Developer options
Keeps working without Wi-Fi
Turn on Mika’s accessibility

Find Mika in your system’s “Accessibility” settings and turn it on. Then Mika reads the pairing code by itself when pairing — no typing needed. You can also skip this (recommended): after pairing, Mika turns it on by itself without being blocked by Android’s “restricted setting”, and this time you enter the code from the notification. If the system says “An app is obscuring a permission request”, close other apps’ floating windows or bubbles and try again.
Open Accessibility settings
Mika reads the pairing code itself
Turn on Wireless debugging

In “Developer options”, find “Wireless debugging” and turn it on. When asked, choose “Allow” and tick “Always allow on this network” so you won’t be asked again. You need to be on Wi-Fi (internet access not required).

Open “Wireless debugging”, then tap “Pair device with pairing code”. A 6-digit code appears on screen.

Not connected to Wi-Fi
Mika needs Wi-Fi to start phone control (no internet needed). It resumes by itself once you join any Wi-Fi.
Wireless debugging isn’t allowed on this Wi-Fi yet

Mika turned on Wireless debugging, but the system didn’t allow it on this Wi-Fi. Turn on “Wireless debugging” once yourself; when asked, tick “Always allow on this network” and tap Allow. After that Mika can turn it on by itself on this Wi-Fi.
Couldn’t connect to Wireless debugging
Couldn’t find the Wireless debugging port. You can: turn “Wireless debugging” off and on again, then retry; switch to a phone hotspot or your home Wi-Fi; or enter the port below.
Wireless debugging address isn’t on this phone
Mika can only connect to an address on this phone. Retry; if this keeps happening, copy the diagnostics.
Pairing expired
The system may have revoked it after a long time unused, or it was removed. Just pair again. Turn on “Disable adb authorization timeout” in Developer options so it won’t expire again.
Pairing key can’t be read
Mika can no longer read the key it used for pairing. Pair again once; Mika will make a new key and the old “mika@…” entry in Paired devices can be removed.
Connected, but couldn’t get ready
Retrying usually fixes it.

Uses wireless debugging to control apps on a virtual screen

After pairing once, Mika’s built-in helper stays in the background and keeps working even without Wi-Fi. Keep “USB debugging” (in Developer options) on; turning it off stops phone control. After a restart, join Wi-Fi and turn on “Wireless debugging” and Mika reconnects by itself — no new code needed.

Unpair?

Mika will delete the pairing, stop using apps on the virtual screen, and revoke the permissions granted through the switches below. Web and file tasks aren’t affected. To use apps again later, you’ll need to pair once more. You can also remove Mika under “Wireless debugging → Paired devices” in system settings.

Run the start command again

Plug the phone into a computer with a USB cable and run this command on the computer (any other way to run this adb command for the phone works too). On most phones it keeps running after you unplug the cable; if it stops, plug in and run the command again to restore phone control. It’s also needed again after every phone restart.

Keep USB debugging on. The helper was started with the USB command. On most phones it keeps running after you unplug the cable; if it stops, plug in and run the command again. After a phone restart, open Mika once and run the command again.

Mika’s built-in helper was started with the USB start command. On most phones it keeps running after you unplug the cable; on some systems unplugging stops it. If that happens, plug in and run the command again to restore phone control. Keep “USB debugging” (in Developer options) on; turning it off stops phone control. After a phone restart the helper doesn’t come back by itself: open Mika and run the command again (you can copy it in “Set up phone control”). If this phone has a working “Wireless debugging”, pairing once lets Mika reconnect by itself after restarts.

Allow root commands?

Root commands can change or delete anything on the phone, including other apps’ data, and can leave the phone unusable. In Ask mode, Mika asks you before each root command that changes or deletes something; in Autonomous mode it doesn’t ask. Turn this on only if you understand the risk.
Allow
This is separate from starting the helper. Turning it on does not let Mika run the helper as root; it only adds root commands to tasks.
Mika found su on this phone. A helper started with root still runs as the same limited user, with the same permissions as one started over Wireless debugging.

Using Shizuku to start Mika’s built-in helper. Once started, phone control works on Wi-Fi or mobile data without Wireless debugging. Mika never starts Shizuku itself; after a phone restart, open Shizuku to start it again (using Wireless debugging only if that is the start method Shizuku uses on this device), and Mika reconnects automatically.
